fact_checks.local_evidence_gap: WSU drought advisory confirms general deficit-irrigation and dormancy-concept for Pacific Northwest alfalfa, but does not reproduce the precise dormancy-regrowth mechanism language or winter-fall cutoff guidance; crop/product is alfalfa but geography is Washington rather than Nebraska/Idaho
fact_checks.quote: Alfalfa is naturally drought tolerant. Its lengthy root systems can reach over 15 feet deep, providing access to a greater soil volume to scavenge water. Alfalfa also has a unique ability to go into drought-induced dormancy when water is scarce. This feature allows for irrigation to cease at almost any time during the growing season without permanent damage to the stand.
fact_checks.scope: Pacific Northwest deficit-irrigation advisory; drought-adaptive dormancy concept supports qualitative dormancy-regrowth general principle; Washington geography and soil/water conditions differ from Nebraska and southern Idaho sources cited by article, so applicability to target countries outside the arid western US is uncertain

fact_checks.local_evidence_gap: PubMed research reports summer deficit-irrigation economics and water-security benefits for southwestern USA; it does not provide dormancy physiology detail or pre-harvest cutoff protocol for other US regions
fact_checks.quote: We demonstrate that adoption of summer deficit irrigation in alfalfa production can yield large water savings and flexibility to adapt to changing water supplies with minimal on-field economic impact. We estimate that deficit irrigation of alfalfa can save 1333 to 4157 million cubic meters of water annually...if summer deficit irrigation suspended after July 1 were implemented.
fact_checks.scope: Southwestern USA summer deficit-irrigation study covering water savings, economic trade-offs, and infrastructure needs; alfalfa crop/product is consistent but climate, season and water-trading context are US southwest only, limiting transfer to general dormancy/regrowth claims for other regions
